messages.content: Can you extend the argument to general p and a, beyond p=n and a=m? State the additional assumptions needed to control the variation terms and prove the corresponding optimal L² estimate theorem.

I’ll check the curvature signs in general bidegree and state a theorem with explicit control of the variation terms. The key issue is that outside top degree, positive line-bundle curvature need not give a positive \(\bar\partial\) curvature operator.

There is a concrete extension for arbitrary fibre bidegree: write \(L\) as a unitary flat bundle tensored with a bundle from the base, and require the base curvature to dominate an explicit bound on the two adjacent Hodge variation maps. This permits nonzero variation. The general-degree estimate must also specify which auxiliary weights have a positive curvature operator, since positivity of the auxiliary line bundle alone no longer suffices.

The estimate can retain the optimal constant \(1\). The variation contributes
\[
R_{j\bar k}=\theta_k^*\theta_j-\eta_j\eta_k^*,
\]
and an explicit curvature bound can absorb its possible negative part. I’ll also state a stronger uniform total-space condition that gives a literal shifted implication; a single fixed-degree optimal estimate does not establish that condition.

**Yes, under explicit bounds on the variation and a degree-dependent curvature condition.** For general \(p\) and \(a\), semipositivity of \(h\) alone is insufficient: both adjacent Hodge components contribute to curvature, and the curvature commutator need not preserve positivity.

I will give a concrete theorem permitting nonzero variation, followed by a version formulated as a shifted total-space implication.

First, the meaning of “optimal \((a,b)\) estimates” needs care. For an auxiliary Hermitian line bundle \(A\), put
\[
B_A^{a,b}=[i\Theta_A,\Lambda_{\omega_Y}]
\quad\text{on }\Lambda^{a,b}T^*Y.
\]
Call \(A\) **admissible in degree \((a,b)\)** when \(B_A^{a,b}>0\). If \(i\Theta_A\) has eigenvalues \(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m\), the eigenvalues of this operator are
\[
\sum_{i\in I}\lambda_i+\sum_{j\in J}\lambda_j
-\sum_{\ell=1}^m\lambda_\ell,
\qquad |I|=a,\quad |J|=b.
\tag{1}
\]
Thus positivity of \(A\) does not suffice in an interior bidegree. Moreover, positive admissible auxiliary bundles can exist only when
\[
a+b>m,
\]
as follows by taking the average of the eigenvalues in (1). The theorem below explicitly uses admissible tests.

**Theorem — quantitative control of harmonic variation.**  
Let
\[
\pi:X\longrightarrow (Y,\omega_Y)
\]
be a smooth proper Kähler fibration, where \(Y\) is complete Kähler of dimension \(m\), with fibres of dimension \(n\). Fix a closed relative Kähler form \(\omega_f\).

Assume that
\[
(L,h)=(U,h_U)\otimes\pi^*(G,h_G),
\tag{2}
\]
where \(U\) is a unitary flat line bundle and \(h_G\) is smooth. For arbitrary \(0\le p,q\le n\), set
\[
E^{p,q}=R^q\pi_*(\Omega^p_{X/Y}\otimes U),
\qquad
\mathcal F=E^{p,q}\otimes G,
\]
with their fibrewise harmonic metrics \(H_0\) and \(H=H_0h_G\).

Let
\[
\theta_j:E^{p,q}\longrightarrow E^{p-1,q+1},
\qquad
\eta_j:E^{p+1,q-1}\longrightarrow E^{p,q}
\tag{3}
\]
be the outgoing and incoming Higgs operators in an \(\omega_Y\)-unitary tangent frame. Define
\[
\kappa(y)=
\sum_{j=1}^m
\left(
\|\theta_j\|_{\mathrm{HS}}^2+
\|\eta_j\|_{\mathrm{HS}}^2
\right).
\tag{4}
\]
Missing Hodge components are interpreted as zero. This quantity is independent of the unitary frame.

Fix \(0\le a\le m\) and \(1\le b\le m\). Let
\[
c_{a,b}(G)
=
\lambda_{\min}\!\left(
[i\Theta_G,\Lambda_{\omega_Y}]_{\Lambda^{a,b}}
\right).
\]
Suppose pointwise on \(Y\) that
\[
\boxed{
c_{a,b}(G)\ge 2m^2\kappa.
}
\tag{5}
\]

Then, for every admissible auxiliary line bundle \((A,h_A)\) and every
\[
f\in A_c^{a,b}(Y,\mathcal F\otimes A),
\qquad \bar\partial f=0,
\]
there exists \(u\in L^2_{a,b-1}(Y,\mathcal F\otimes A)\) satisfying
\[
\boxed{
\bar\partial u=f,\qquad
\int_Y|u|_{H\otimes h_A}^2\,dV_Y
\le
\int_Y
\left\langle(B_A^{a,b})^{-1}f,f\right\rangle_{H\otimes h_A}
\,dV_Y.
}
\tag{6}
\]
In particular, this applies to positive admissible auxiliary bundles in the range \(a+b>m\), with no restriction \(p=n\) or \(a=m\).

**Proof.**

**1. Identify the metric and the variation operators.**

Because \(U\) is unitary flat, its fibre cohomology carries the Hodge decomposition. The fixed relative Kähler class supplies the polarized Lefschetz decomposition; its Hodge metric, with the corresponding normalization on each summand, is the fibrewise harmonic \(L^2\) metric.

The projection formula gives
\[
(\mathcal F,H)
=
(E^{p,q},H_0)\otimes(G,h_G).
\tag{7}
\]
Indeed, \(h_G(y)\) is constant along \(X_y\), so it changes the fibrewise norm by a scalar without changing harmonic representatives.

The operators in (3) measure the variation of those representatives. For example,
\[
\theta_j[\alpha]
=
\left[
\operatorname{KS}(\partial_{y^j})\mathbin{\lrcorner}\alpha
\right],
\tag{8}
\]
whose harmonic representative is obtained by fibrewise harmonic projection.

Let \(D\) be the direct sum of the Chern connections of the Hodge bundles. The Gauss–Manin connection decomposes as
\[
\nabla=D+\theta+\theta^\dagger.
\]
Taking the Hodge-degree-preserving part of \(\nabla^2=0\) gives
\[
\boxed{
R^{E^{p,q}}_{j\bar k}
=
\theta_k^\dagger\theta_j-\eta_j\eta_k^\dagger.
}
\tag{9}
\]
This is the exact curvature contribution of harmonic variation. See [Sabbah–Schnell, §50, Proposition (b)](https://www.math.stonybrook.edu/~cschnell/pdf/papers/VHS-disk.pdf).

The second term is absent in an extreme Hodge degree, but generally survives. Even the first term must be passed through the degree-\((a,b)\) commutator before its sign can be assessed.

**2. Bound the full variation contribution.**

Write
\[
\mathscr V_{a,b}
=
[i\Theta_{E^{p,q},H_0},\Lambda_{\omega_Y}]
\quad\text{on }\Lambda^{a,b}T^*Y\otimes E^{p,q}.
\tag{10}
\]
From (9),
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{j,k}\|R_{j\bar k}\|_{\mathrm{op}}
&\le
\left(\sum_j\|\theta_j\|_{\mathrm{HS}}\right)^2
+
\left(\sum_j\|\eta_j\|_{\mathrm{HS}}\right)^2\\
&\le m\kappa.
\end{aligned}
\]
Exterior multiplication by a unit elementary two-form has operator norm at most \(1\), and \(\|\Lambda_{\omega_Y}\|\le m\). Therefore
\[
\boxed{
\|\mathscr V_{a,b}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le 2m^2\kappa.
}
\tag{11}
\]
This deliberately nonsharp bound controls both adjacent Hodge components, including all their cross terms.

**3. Absorb variation into the curvature of \(G\).**

By (7),
\[
[i\Theta_{\mathcal F,H},\Lambda_{\omega_Y}]
=
[i\Theta_G,\Lambda_{\omega_Y}]\otimes\operatorname{Id}
+
\mathscr V_{a,b}.
\]
Consequently, (5) and (11) imply
\[
\boxed{
[i\Theta_{\mathcal F,H},\Lambda_{\omega_Y}]
\ge0
\quad\text{in degree }(a,b).
}
\tag{12}
\]

The more precise hypothesis, of which (5) is a convenient sufficient criterion, is
\[
\boxed{
[i\Theta_G,\Lambda_{\omega_Y}]\otimes\operatorname{Id}
+
\left[
i\sum_{j,k}
(\theta_k^\dagger\theta_j-\eta_j\eta_k^\dagger)
\,dy^j\wedge d\bar y^k,
\Lambda_{\omega_Y}
\right]
\ge0.
}
\tag{13}
\]
This formula specifies exactly which variation terms must be controlled.

**4. Solve with the optimal constant.**

For \(\mathcal F\otimes A\)-valued \((a,b)\)-forms, the Bochner–Kodaira identity and (12) give
\[
\begin{aligned}
\|\bar\partial v\|^2+\|\bar\partial^*v\|^2
&=
\|D'v\|^2+\|(D')^*v\|^2\\
&\quad+
\int_Y
\left\langle
\bigl([i\Theta_{\mathcal F,H},\Lambda]+B_A^{a,b}\bigr)v,v
\right\rangle\\
&\ge
\int_Y\langle B_A^{a,b}v,v\rangle.
\end{aligned}
\tag{14}
\]
The identity holds in arbitrary bidegree; see [Demailly, *Analytic Methods in Algebraic Geometry*, Chapters 4–5](https://www-fourier.univ-grenoble-alpes.fr/~demailly/manuscripts/analmeth_book.pdf).

Let
\[
R(f)=\int_Y\langle(B_A^{a,b})^{-1}f,f\rangle.
\]
Weighted Cauchy–Schwarz gives
\[
|(f,v)|^2
\le R(f)\int_Y\langle B_A^{a,b}v,v\rangle.
\]
For \(\bar\partial\)-closed \(v\), (14) therefore yields
\[
|(f,v)|^2\le R(f)\|\bar\partial^*v\|^2.
\]
Completeness and the Hilbert-space existence argument for \(\bar\partial\) produce \(u\) with
\[
\bar\partial u=f,\qquad \|u\|^2\le R(f).
\]
This proves (6), with constant \(1\). \(\square\)

The hypothesis is quite concrete. If the smallest and largest eigenvalues of \(i\Theta_G\) are \(\lambda_{\min}\) and \(\lambda_{\max}\), then
\[
c_{a,b}(G)\ge
b\lambda_{\min}-(m-a)\lambda_{\max}.
\]
Hence it suffices that
\[
b\lambda_{\min}-(m-a)\lambda_{\max}\ge2m^2\kappa.
\tag{15}
\]
In particular, if
\[
i\Theta_G=\lambda\omega_Y,
\]
condition (5) becomes
\[
\boxed{
\lambda(a+b-m)\ge2m^2\kappa.
}
\tag{16}
\]
For instance, on a compact projective base, one can take \(\omega_Y=i\Theta_{A_0}\) for a positive line bundle \(A_0\), and \(G=A_0^N\) with \(N\) sufficiently large. This permits arbitrary fibre bidegrees and interior base bidegrees such as \((a,b)=(2,2)\) when \(m=3\).

There is also a precise **shifted total-space version**. Keep the hypotheses (2) and suppose \(X\) has a Kähler form \(\omega_X\). Set
\[
\Omega_\varepsilon=\pi^*\omega_Y+\varepsilon\omega_X.
\]
Assume that a nonnegative function \(\nu\) satisfies
\[
\mathscr V_{a,b}\ge-\nu\,\operatorname{Id},
\tag{17}
\]
and, for a sequence \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\),
\[
\boxed{
[i\Theta_{L,h},\Lambda_{\Omega_\varepsilon}]
\ge(\nu\circ\pi)\operatorname{Id}
\quad\text{on }\Lambda^{a+p,b+q}T^*X\otimes L.
}
\tag{18}
\]
Then the same optimal estimate (6) follows.

Indeed, \(U\) is flat, so \(i\Theta_L=\pi^*i\Theta_G\). Restrict (18) to the component with horizontal degree \((a,b)\) and vertical degree \((p,q)\). The commutator acts there through the horizontal metric alone. As \(\varepsilon\to0\), this metric converges to \(\pi^*\omega_Y\), giving
\[
[i\Theta_G,\Lambda_{\omega_Y}]
\ge\nu\,\operatorname{Id}.
\]
Combining this with (17) proves (12), and the preceding \(L^2\) argument applies.

Condition (18) is a uniform, quantitative strengthening of the total-space positivity assumption. A single optimal estimate in degree \((a+p,b+q)\) does not establish it automatically. Outside canonical degree, adjacent harmonic types have the same total fibre degree, so their contributions need not disappear under fibre rescaling. Equations (9), (13), and (17) explicitly control those surviving terms.

Can you remove the assumption that L is a unitary flat bundle tensored with a pullback, and treat a general smooth semipositive (L,h)? State sufficient conditions controlling harmonic variation and prove the optimal L² estimate.

I’ll formulate conditions directly in terms of the fibrewise harmonic projections and their variation, so they apply to a general smooth semipositive \(L\). I’ll distinguish the positivity supplied by \(h\) from the additional control needed for the induced metric.

A useful sufficient criterion has three parts: constant fibre cohomology dimension, a spectral gap for the fibrewise Dolbeault Laplacian, and an ambient curvature lower bound large enough to absorb the variation of the harmonic projections. The Green operator gives that variation explicitly. This allows arbitrary vertical and mixed curvature of \(L\), but the ambient lower bound remains an additional hypothesis.

Yes. **The flatness assumption can be replaced by a quantitative bound on the variation of the fibrewise Dolbeault Laplacian, together with a curvature lower bound that absorbs this variation.** This permits arbitrary smooth semipositive \(L\), including nonzero vertical and mixed curvature.

Semipositivity of \(L\) alone does not provide these additional bounds. The theorem below is a sufficient criterion, rather than an unconditional positivity theorem for all higher direct images. General curvature formulas for these twisted direct images are studied by [Choi–Schumacher](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.04298).

**Set-up and the ambient connection.** Let
\[
\pi:X\longrightarrow (Y,\omega_Y)
\]
be a smooth proper Kähler fibration, with \(\dim Y=m\) and fibres of dimension \(n\). Fix a smooth family of fibrewise Kähler metrics \(\omega_y\), and let \((L,h)\) be a holomorphic line bundle with smooth metric satisfying
\[
i\Theta_{L,h}\ge0.
\]

Fix \(0\le p,q\le n\), and assume
\[
\dim H^q(X_y,\Omega^p_{X_y}\otimes L_y)
\]
is locally constant. Then
\[
\mathcal F=R^q\pi_*(\Omega^p_{X/Y}\otimes L)
\]
is locally free, with harmonic metric
\[
H_y(u,v)
=
\int_{X_y}
\langle \alpha_u,\alpha_v\rangle_{\omega_y,h_y}
\frac{\omega_y^n}{n!}.
\]

Write
\[
\mathscr A_y=A^{p,q}(X_y,L_y),\qquad
\Delta_y=\Box''_y,\qquad
P_[local path omitted]
\]
and put \(Q_y=I-P_y\). The harmonic bundle
\[
\mathcal H=\ker\Delta
\]
identifies isometrically with \((\mathcal F,H)\).

We need a connection on \(\mathscr A\) constructed **before projecting to harmonic forms**. Choose a smooth complex horizontal splitting of \(\pi\). Apply it to the Dolbeault resolution of the holomorphic bundle
\[
\mathscr E=\Omega^p_{X/Y}\otimes L
\]
on \(X\). Its Dolbeault operator decomposes as
\[
\bar\partial_{\mathscr E}
=
d_v+D_h''+\mathcal R_h,
\]
where the changes in horizontal and vertical antiholomorphic degrees are respectively
\[
(0,1),\qquad (1,0),\qquad (2,-1).
\]
In particular,
\[
d_vD_h''+D_h''d_v=0.
\]
Thus \(D_h''\) induces the canonical Dolbeault operator on fibre cohomology.

Let \(D\) be the connection on smooth fibrewise forms whose \((0,1)\)-part is \(D_h''\) and which is compatible with the fibrewise \(L^2\) metric. Its \((1,0)\)-part is determined by metric compatibility, using formal fibrewise adjoints. Consequently,
\[
D^{\mathcal F}=PD|_{\mathcal H}
\]
is precisely the Chern connection of \(H\).

Here \(D\) acts on smooth fibrewise forms; we do not require its coefficients to be bounded operators on the entire fibrewise \(L^2\) space.

**Theorem.** Suppose \(Y\) is complete Kähler. Fix
\[
0\le a\le m,\qquad 1\le b\le m.
\]
Use the connection \(D\) above and assume the following pointwise conditions.

First, the fibre Laplacian has a spectral gap:
\[
\Delta_y|_{\mathcal H_y^\perp}\ge \gamma(y)I,
\qquad \gamma(y)>0.
\tag{1}
\]

In an \(\omega_Y\)-unitary frame \(e_1,\dots,e_m\), define
\[
T_j=[D_{e_j},\Delta]P,\qquad
T_{\bar j}=[D_{\bar e_j},\Delta]P,
\]
and
\[
\mathfrak d(y)
=
\sum_{j=1}^m
\left(
\|T_j\|_{\mathrm{HS}}^2+
\|T_{\bar j}\|_{\mathrm{HS}}^2
\right).
\tag{2}
\]
These operators have finite-dimensional domain \(\mathcal H_y\), so the indicated norms are well-defined.

Write the \((1,1)\)-curvature of \(D\) as
\[
(D^2)^{1,1}
=
\sum_{j,k}R^D_{j\bar k}\,\zeta^j\wedge\bar\zeta^k.
\]
Define the compressed ambient curvature commutator
\[
\mathcal K^{a,b}
=
\left[
i\sum_{j,k}
P R^D_{j\bar k}P\,
\zeta^j\wedge\bar\zeta^k,
\Lambda_{\omega_Y}
\right]_{\Lambda^{a,b}T_Y^*\otimes\mathcal H}.
\tag{3}
\]

Assume the curvature domination condition
\[
\boxed{
\mathcal K^{a,b}
\ \ge\
\frac{2m^2}{\gamma^2}\,\mathfrak d\;I.
}
\tag{4}
\]

Then
\[
\boxed{
[i\Theta_{\mathcal F,H},\Lambda_{\omega_Y}]_{a,b}\ge0.
}
\tag{5}
\]

Consequently, let \((A,h_A)\) be any smooth Hermitian holomorphic line bundle on \(Y\) for which
\[
B_A
=
[i\Theta_{A,h_A},\Lambda_{\omega_Y}]_{a,b}
\otimes I_{\mathcal F}>0.
\tag{6}
\]
For every \(\bar\partial\)-closed
\[
f\in L^2_{a,b}(Y,\mathcal F\otimes A)
\]
such that
\[
\mathcal I(f)
:=
\int_Y\langle B_A^{-1}f,f\rangle_{H\otimes h_A,\omega_Y}
\,dV_{\omega_Y}<\infty,
\]
there exists
\[
u\in L^2_{a,b-1}(Y,\mathcal F\otimes A)
\]
satisfying
\[
\boxed{
\bar\partial u=f,\qquad
\int_Y|u|^2_{H\otimes h_A,\omega_Y}\,dV_{\omega_Y}
\le
\mathcal I(f).
}
\tag{7}
\]

Thus \(H\) satisfies the optimal \((a,b)\)-\(L^2\) estimate, with constant \(1\), for the admissible auxiliary metrics in (6).

The spectral gap in (1) is locally available from compactness of the fibres and constancy of the harmonic dimension. The substantive additional hypothesis is the domination in (4).

**Proof.**

**1. Express harmonic variation through the Green operator.**

Let
\[
G_y=(\Delta_y|_{\mathcal H_y^\perp})^{-1}Q_y.
\]
Then
\[
\|G_y\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\gamma(y)^{-1}.
\]

The two components of the second fundamental form of the harmonic subbundle are
\[
B_j=QD_{e_j}|_{\mathcal H},\qquad
C_j=QD_{\bar e_j}|_{\mathcal H}.
\tag{8}
\]

For a smooth harmonic section \(s\), differentiating \(\Delta s=0\) gives
\[
\Delta D_{e_j}s=-[D_{e_j},\Delta]s.
\]
Applying \(G\) yields
\[
\boxed{
B_j=-GT_j,\qquad C_j=-GT_{\bar j}.
}
\tag{9}
\]
Therefore, if
\[
\kappa
=
\sum_j
\left(
\|B_j\|_{\mathrm{HS}}^2+
\|C_j\|_{\mathrm{HS}}^2
\right),
\]
then
\[
\boxed{\kappa\le\gamma^{-2}\mathfrak d.}
\tag{10}
\]

Formula (9) incorporates the variation of the complex structures, fibre metrics, relative holomorphic forms, and the metric on \(L\). It requires no flat connection on \(L\).

**2. Compute the curvature of the harmonic metric.**

With respect to the orthogonal decomposition
\[
\mathscr A=\mathcal H\oplus\mathcal H^\perp,
\]
metric compatibility gives the block form
\[
D=
\begin{pmatrix}
D^{\mathcal F}&-S^\dagger\\
S&D^\perp
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
S=\sum_j(B_j\zeta^j+C_j\bar\zeta^j).
\]
Computing its curvature gives
\[
\Theta_{\mathcal F,H}=PD^2P+S^\dagger\wedge S.
\]
In components,
\[
\boxed{
R^{\mathcal F}_{j\bar k}
=
P R^D_{j\bar k}P
-
B_k^\dagger B_j
+
C_j^\dagger C_k.
}
\tag{11}
\]

Both variation terms matter in arbitrary bidegree. In particular, one cannot discard the \(C\)-term merely because it has a plus sign before taking the curvature commutator.

This is where the defects of a naive total-space harmonic lift are accounted for: the lift is isometric, but need not be a closed ordinary \(L\)-valued form on \(X\). The projection-curvature calculation retains its variation terms explicitly. 

**3. Bound the variation contribution.**

Set
\[
V_{j\bar k}=-B_k^\dagger B_j+C_j^\dagger C_k.
\]
Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{j,k}\|V_{j\bar k}\|_{\mathrm{op}}
&\le
\left(\sum_j\|B_j\|_{\mathrm{HS}}\right)^2
+
\left(\sum_j\|C_j\|_{\mathrm{HS}}\right)^2\\
&\le m\kappa.
\end{aligned}
\tag{12}
\]
Exterior multiplication by a unit elementary two-form has norm at most \(1\), and
\[
\|\Lambda_{\omega_Y}\|\le m.
\]
Hence
\[
\left\|
\left[
i\sum_{j,k}V_{j\bar k}\zeta^j\wedge\bar\zeta^k,
\Lambda_{\omega_Y}
\right]
\right\|_{\mathrm{op}}
\le 2m^2\kappa.
\tag{13}
\]

Combining (10), (11), and (13),
\[
\begin{aligned}
[i\Theta_{\mathcal F,H},\Lambda_{\omega_Y}]_{a,b}
&\ge \mathcal K^{a,b}-2m^2\kappa I\\
&\ge \mathcal K^{a,b}
-\frac{2m^2}{\gamma^2}\mathfrak d\,I\\
&\ge0.
\end{aligned}
\]
This proves (5).

The constant \(2m^2\) is a convenient sufficient bound, not a sharp bound for harmonic variation. The resulting \(L^2\) estimate nevertheless has the exact constant \(1\).

**4. Solve \(\bar\partial\) with the optimal estimate.**

For compactly supported smooth \(\mathcal F\otimes A\)-valued \((a,b)\)-forms \(v\), the Bochner–Kodaira–Nakano identity gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\|\bar\partial v\|^2+\|\bar\partial^*v\|^2
&=
\|D'v\|^2+\|(D')^*v\|^2\\
&\quad+
\int_Y
\left\langle
[i\Theta_{\mathcal F,H},\Lambda_{\omega_Y}]v,v
\right\rangle\,dV_{\omega_Y}\\
&\quad+
\int_Y\langle B_Av,v\rangle\,dV_{\omega_Y}\\
&\ge
\int_Y\langle B_Av,v\rangle\,dV_{\omega_Y}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{14}
\]
Completeness permits extension to the relevant operator domains.

For \(v\in\ker\bar\partial\cap\operatorname{Dom}\bar\partial^*\), weighted Cauchy–Schwarz gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
|(f,v)|^2
&\le
\mathcal I(f)
\int_Y\langle B_Av,v\rangle\,dV_{\omega_Y}\\
&\le \mathcal I(f)\|\bar\partial^*v\|^2.
\end{aligned}
\tag{15}
\]
Hilbert-space duality now produces \(u\) with
\[
\bar\partial u=f,\qquad \|u\|^2\le\mathcal I(f).
\]
This is the standard complete-Kähler existence argument; see [Demailly, Chapters 4–5](https://www-fourier.univ-grenoble-alpes.fr/~demailly/manuscripts/analmeth_book.pdf). \(\square\)

**How the hypotheses can be realized for a nonflat \(L\).** The ambient operator \(\mathcal K^{a,b}\) contains contributions from the relative cotangent bundle, horizontal splitting, fibre volume, and \(h\). Thus \(i\Theta_{L,h}\ge0\) does not by itself imply (4). Nevertheless, the criterion can hold for genuinely nonflat twists.

For example, suppose \(Y\) is compact projective, and choose a positive line bundle \(A_0\) with
\[
i\Theta_{A_0}=\omega_Y.
\]
Start with any smooth semipositive \((L_0,h_0)\) having constant relevant cohomology dimensions, and put
\[
(L_N,h_N)
=
(L_0,h_0)\otimes\pi^*(A_0,h_{A_0})^{\otimes N}.
\]
Here \(L_0\) may have arbitrary nonzero vertical and mixed curvature.

The pullback factor scales each fibre metric by a scalar. Consequently, the fibre Laplacians and harmonic projections are unchanged, and so are the off-diagonal operators \(B_j,C_j\). Meanwhile,
\[
\mathcal K_N^{a,b}
=
\mathcal K_0^{a,b}
+
N(a+b-m)I.
\tag{16}
\]
Choose constants \(C,K\ge0\) such that
\[
\mathcal K_0^{a,b}\ge-CI,\qquad \kappa\le K.
\]
When \(a+b>m\), the condition
\[
N(a+b-m)\ge C+2m^2K
\tag{17}
\]
therefore guarantees the optimal estimate. This example imposes no unitary-flat factorization on \(L_0\).

Finally, the auxiliary positivity condition (6) is essential for general degrees. If \(i\Theta_A\) has eigenvalues \(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_m\), then \(B_A\) has eigenvalues
\[
\sum_{i\in I}\lambda_i+\sum_{j\in J}\lambda_j
-\sum_{\ell=1}^m\lambda_\ell,
\qquad |I|=a,\quad |J|=b.
\]
Thus positivity of \(A\) alone does not ensure \(B_A>0\). If the definition requires positive auxiliary line bundles, admissible tests can exist only when \(a+b>m\). The theorem applies to every \(p,q,a,b\) in the stated ranges, subject to this explicit admissibility condition.

Can you express the curvature domination condition (4) explicitly in terms of the curvature of L and the Kodaira–Spencer tensors, and give a nonisotrivial example satisfying it without adding a large pullback twist?

I’ll check how the domination condition expands in a general twisted family, including which terms involve more than the curvature of \(L\) and the Kodaira–Spencer tensors. I’ll also look for a nonisotrivial example where the condition holds without a large pullback twist.

There is a concrete example: a varying elliptic curve times \(\mathbb P^1\), with \(L\) equal to \(\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(1)\) on the second factor. Its direct-image metric has positive curvature, and the error term in condition (4) vanishes. The Kodaira–Spencer tensor is nonzero; in this example it supplies the positive curvature.

Yes. **There is an explicit expansion, and a nonisotrivial example satisfying the literal condition (4) with nonflat \(L\) and strictly positive \(H\), without any pullback twist.**

One qualification is necessary: condition (4) depends on the chosen relative Kähler geometry and fibrewise spectral data. In general, it cannot be reduced to an inequality involving only the pointwise curvature of \(L\) and the norm of the Kodaira–Spencer tensor.

**1. Expand the geometric quantities entering (4).**

Fix a closed real \((1,1)\)-form \(\omega_X\) whose restrictions to the fibres are Kähler. Use its horizontal lifts
\[
v_i=\frac{\partial}{\partial s^i}
+a_i^\alpha\frac{\partial}{\partial z^\alpha}.
\]
Write
\[
A_i=\bar\partial_{X_y}v_i
=
\frac{\partial a_i^\alpha}{\partial\bar z^\beta}
\,d\bar z^\beta\otimes\frac{\partial}{\partial z^\alpha}
\]
for the corresponding Kodaira–Spencer representatives.

Let \(\Theta_L\) denote the Chern curvature, with \(i\Theta_L\ge0\). Besides its horizontal component, we need its mixed component
\[
\eta_i
=
-\left(\iota_{v_i}\Theta_L\right)\big|_{X_y}.
\tag{18}
\]
For example, if \(h=e^{-\varphi}\), then
\[
\eta_i
=
-\left(
\varphi_{i\bar\beta}
+a_i^\alpha\varphi_{\alpha\bar\beta}
\right)d\bar z^\beta,
\]
and
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Theta_L(v_i,\bar v_j)
={}&\varphi_{i\bar j}
+a_i^\alpha\varphi_{\alpha\bar j}
+\bar a_j^\beta\varphi_{i\bar\beta}\\
&+a_i^\alpha\bar a_j^\beta\varphi_{\alpha\bar\beta}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{19}
\]

Define the standard insertion operator
\[
\mathsf C_i
=
\sum_{\alpha,\beta}
(A_i)^\alpha_{\bar\beta}
\,d\bar z^\beta\wedge\iota_{\partial/\partial z^\alpha}.
\tag{20}
\]
It maps \((p,q)\)-forms to \((p-1,q+1)\)-forms. Its fibrewise adjoint is denoted by \(\mathsf C_i^\dagger\).

All operators below act on fibrewise \(L\)-valued forms. Put
\[
\boxed{
W_i=\eta_i\wedge-[\partial_h,\mathsf C_i],
}
\tag{21}
\]
where the bracket is the ordinary commutator. Thus
\[
W_i u
=
\eta_i\wedge u
-\partial_h(\mathsf C_i u)
+\mathsf C_i(\partial_hu).
\]
Its adjoint is
\[
W_i^\dagger
=
(\eta_i\wedge)^\dagger
+[\partial_h^*,\mathsf C_i^\dagger].
\tag{22}
\]
On input degree \((p,q)\), \(W_i^\dagger\) means the adjoint of \(W_i\) acting on degree \((p,q-1)\).

These formulas display the two sources of variation: the mixed curvature of \(L\), and the Kodaira–Spencer action together with its vertical derivatives.

For the connection \(D\) in the preceding answer, using this horizontal splitting, the compressed ambient curvature is
\[
\boxed{
M_{i\bar j}:=PR^D_{i\bar j}P
=
P\left(
\Theta_L(v_i,\bar v_j)
+\mathcal L^h_{[v_i,\bar v_j]}
+[\mathsf C_j^\dagger,\mathsf C_i]
\right)P.
}
\tag{23}
\]
Here \(\mathcal L^h\) is the covariant Lie derivative using the Chern connection of \(L\).

In particular, for a tangent direction \(\xi\) and a harmonic form \(u\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
\langle M_{\xi\bar\xi}u,u\rangle
={}&
\langle\Theta_L(v_\xi,\bar v_\xi)u,u\rangle
+\langle\mathcal L^h_{[v_\xi,\bar v_\xi]}u,u\rangle\\
&+\|\mathsf C_\xi u\|^2
-\|\mathsf C_\xi^\dagger u\|^2.
\end{aligned}
\tag{24}
\]
The general direct-image curvature formula, including these geometric terms and the Green-operator corrections, is developed in [Choi–Schumacher, Main Theorem 1 and §§5–8](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.04298v1).

The bracket term is an additional geometric contribution. If
\[
c_{i\bar j}
=
g_{i\bar j}
-g_{i\bar\beta}g^{\bar\beta\alpha}g_{\alpha\bar j}
\]
is the geodesic curvature of \(\omega_X\), then
\[
[v_i,\bar v_j]
=
g^{\bar\beta\alpha}
\frac{\partial c_{i\bar j}}{\partial\bar z^\beta}
\frac{\partial}{\partial z^\alpha}
-
g^{\bar\beta\alpha}
\frac{\partial c_{i\bar j}}{\partial z^\alpha}
\frac{\partial}{\partial\bar z^\beta}.
\tag{25}
\]
Thus this term involves vertical derivatives of the geodesic curvature.

If \(L\) is strictly positive along the fibres, one can choose
\[
\omega_X=i\Theta_L.
\]
Then \(\eta_i=0\), and \(c_{i\bar j}\) is the Schur complement of the vertical curvature matrix of \(L\). In that case the formulas are determined by the curvature geometry of \(L\), the Kodaira–Spencer representatives, and the associated fibrewise operators.

**2. The explicit version of condition (4).**

Let \(\{u_\nu\}\) be an orthonormal basis of the harmonic space \(\mathcal H_y^{p,q}(L_y)\). Take the base frame to be \(\omega_Y\)-unitary, and define
\[
\boxed{
\mathcal E(y)
=
\sum_{i,\nu}
\left(
\|\bar\partial^*W_i u_\nu\|^2
+
\|\bar\partial W_i^\dagger u_\nu\|^2
\right).
}
\tag{26}
\]
Then the literal condition (4), for this choice of horizontal connection, becomes
\[
\boxed{
\left[
i\sum_{i,j}M_{i\bar j}\,
\zeta^i\wedge\bar\zeta^j,\Lambda_{\omega_Y}
\right]_{a,b}
\ge
\frac{2m^2}{\gamma(y)^2}\,\mathcal E(y)\,I.
}
\tag{27}
\]
Here \(M\) is explicitly given by (23), and \(\gamma(y)\) is a lower bound for the positive spectrum of \(\Delta_{p,q,y}\).

To verify this identification, the covariant Cartan identities give
\[
[\bar\partial,D_i]=W_i,
\qquad
[\bar\partial^*,D_{\bar i}]=W_i^\dagger,
\]
while
\[
[\bar\partial^*,D_i]=0,\qquad
[\bar\partial,D_{\bar i}]=0.
\]
Therefore, for harmonic \(u\),
\[
\Delta D_i u=\bar\partial^*W_i u,
\qquad
\Delta D_{\bar i}u=\bar\partial W_i^\dagger u.
\]
Since \(\Delta u=0\),
\[
[D_i,\Delta]u=-\bar\partial^*W_i u,
\qquad
[D_{\bar i},\Delta]u=-\bar\partial W_i^\dagger u.
\]
Consequently, \(\mathcal E=\mathfrak d\), exactly as required.

A less restrictive sufficient condition avoids the coarse spectral-gap estimate. Define
\[
\begin{aligned}
\kappa
=\sum_{i,\nu}\bigl(
&\langle G_{p,q+1}W_i u_\nu,W_i u_\nu\rangle\\
&+\langle G_{p,q-1}W_i^\dagger u_\nu,W_i^\dagger u_\nu\rangle
\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\tag{28}
\]
Terms in nonexistent degrees are zero. It suffices to require the left side of (27) to dominate \(2m^2\kappa I\).

Indeed, these Green energies are precisely the squared norms of the off-diagonal harmonic variations:
\[
QD_i u=\bar\partial^*G_{p,q+1}W_i u,
\qquad
QD_{\bar i}u=\bar\partial G_{p,q-1}W_i^\dagger u.
\]
The Gauss formula and the preceding curvature estimate then give
\[
[i\Theta_{\mathcal F,H},\Lambda_{\omega_Y}]_{a,b}\ge0.
\]
On a complete Kähler base, the Bochner–Kodaira argument yields
\[
\bar\partial u=f,\qquad
\|u\|^2
\le
\int_Y\langle B_A^{-1}f,f\rangle\,dV_{\omega_Y},
\]
for every admissible auxiliary metric with \(B_A>0\), with optimal constant \(1\).

**3. A nonisotrivial example satisfying (27), without a pullback twist.**

Let \(Y=\mathbb H\), with coordinate \(\tau\), and consider the elliptic family
\[
E_\tau=\mathbb C/(\mathbb Z+\tau\mathbb Z).
\]
Write
\[
t=\operatorname{Im}\tau,\qquad r=\operatorname{Im}z.
\]
On its total space, the form
\[
\Omega_E
=
i\partial\bar\partial\frac{r^2}{t}
=
\frac{i}{2t}
\left(dz-\frac rt\,d\tau\right)
\wedge
\left(d\bar z-\frac rt\,d\bar\tau\right)
\tag{29}
\]
is invariant under the lattice, closed, and semipositive. Its restriction to each elliptic fibre has area \(1\).

Set
\[
X=E\times\mathbb P^1,\qquad
\pi:X\longrightarrow\mathbb H,
\]
and take
\[
L=\operatorname{pr}_{\mathbb P^1}^{*}\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(1)
\]
with its Fubini–Study metric. Use the fibre metrics
\[
\omega_\tau=\Omega_E|_{E_\tau}+\omega_{\mathrm{FS}}.
\]

Thus \(L\) is smooth semipositive and nonflat. Its restriction to the \(\mathbb P^1\) factor has degree \(1\), so it cannot be unitary flat tensored with a pullback from \(Y\).

The horizontal lift is
\[
v_\tau=\partial_\tau+\frac rt\,\partial_z,
\]
and
\[
[v_\tau,\bar v_\tau]=0,\qquad
A_\tau
=
\frac{i}{2t}\,d\bar z\otimes\partial_z\ne0.
\tag{30}
\]
The elliptic family, and hence \(\pi\), is nonisotrivial.

Choose
\[
p=1,\qquad q=0.
\]
Notice that \(p<n=2\). Since
\[
H^0\!\left(\mathbb P^1,
\Omega^1_{\mathbb P^1}\otimes\mathcal O(1)\right)=0,
\]
we have
\[
\mathcal F
=
\pi_*(\Omega^1_{X/Y}\otimes L)
\simeq
(\pi_{E*}K_{E/Y})
\otimes H^0(\mathbb P^1,\mathcal O(1)).
\tag{31}
\]
It has rank \(2\).

For a fixed orthonormal basis \(\sigma_1,\sigma_2\) of
\(H^0(\mathbb P^1,\mathcal O(1))\), a holomorphic harmonic frame is
\[
u_\nu=dz\otimes\sigma_\nu.
\]
Here \(dz\) denotes the relative differential. Because \(|dz|^2=2t\), the harmonic metric is
\[
\boxed{H(\tau)=2t\,I_2.}
\tag{32}
\]
Consequently,
\[
\boxed{
i\Theta_{\mathcal F,H}
=
-i\partial\bar\partial\log t\,I_2
=
\frac{i\,d\tau\wedge d\bar\tau}{4t^2}\,I_2.
}
\tag{33}
\]

Crucially, we can verify the stronger ambient condition, rather than merely checking this final curvature. The ambient connection satisfies
\[
D_{\bar\tau}u_\nu=0,\qquad
D_\tau u_\nu=\frac{1}{2it}\,u_\nu.
\tag{34}
\]
It therefore preserves the harmonic subspace:
\[
QD_\tau P=QD_{\bar\tau}P=0.
\]
Hence
\[
\mathcal E=\mathfrak d=\kappa=0.
\tag{35}
\]

The same conclusion follows directly from (21): \(\eta_\tau=0\), and the insertion acts only in the elliptic direction, giving
\[
\partial_h(\mathsf C_\tau u_\nu)
=
\mathsf C_\tau(\partial_hu_\nu).
\]
Thus \(W_\tau u_\nu=0\).

In (23), both the horizontal curvature of \(L\) and the bracket term vanish. Since \(q=0\), \(\mathsf C_\tau^\dagger u_\nu=0\), and therefore
\[
M_{\tau\bar\tau}
=
P\mathsf C_\tau^\dagger\mathsf C_\tau P
=
\frac{1}{4t^2}\,I_2.
\tag{36}
\]
The positive curvature comes entirely from the Kodaira–Spencer term.

Equip \(Y\) with the complete metric
\[
\omega_Y=\frac{i\,d\tau\wedge d\bar\tau}{t^2}.
\]
For base degree \((a,b)=(1,1)\), condition (27) reads
\[
\boxed{
\mathcal K^{1,1}=\frac14 I_2
\ \ge\
\frac{2}{\gamma^2}\mathcal E\,I_2=0.
}
\tag{37}
\]
Thus this example satisfies the original condition (4), and \(H\) satisfies the optimal \((1,1)\)-\(L^2\) estimate. No pullback twist has been added.

If an example with **both \(p<n\) and \(a<m\)** is desired, pull the same family back to \(Y=\mathbb H\times\mathbb H\), with variation only in the first coordinate, and take
\[
(p,q)=(1,0),\qquad (a,b)=(1,2).
\]
The variation error remains zero, while \(\mathcal K^{1,2}\) has eigenvalues \(1/4\) and \(0\). Condition (4) still holds.

Theorem. Let \((Y,\omega_Y)\) be a complete Kähler manifold of dimension \(m\), admitting a positive holomorphic Hermitian line bundle. Let \((Z,\omega_Z)\) be a smooth projective manifold of dimension \(n\). Set
\[
X=Y\times Z,\qquad
\pi=\operatorname{pr}_Y,\qquad
\omega_X=\operatorname{pr}_Y^*\omega_Y+\operatorname{pr}_Z^*\omega_Z.
\]

Suppose that
\[
(L,h)=
\operatorname{pr}_Y^*(G,h_G)\otimes
\operatorname{pr}_Z^*(M,h_M),
\]

where both metrics are smooth.
Fix integers \(a,b,p,q\) in either of the following ranges:
\[
\begin{array}{ll}
\textnormal{(i)}&
a=m,\quad p=n,\quad 1\le b\le m,\quad 0\le q\le n;\\[2mm]
\textnormal{(ii)}&
b=m,\quad q=n,\quad 1\le a\le m,\quad 0\le p\le n.
\end{array}
\]

Equip
\[
\mathcal F=R^q\pi_*(\Omega^p_{X/Y}\otimes L)
\]

with its fibrewise harmonic \(L^2\) metric \(H\), using \(\omega_Z\) and \(h|_{X_y}\).
If \((L,h)\) satisfies the optimal
\[
(a+p,b+q)\text{-}L^2
\]

estimate condition with respect to \(\omega_X\), then \((\mathcal F,H)\) satisfies the optimal
\[
(a,b)\text{-}L^2
\]

estimate condition with respect to \(\omega_Y\).
In particular, case (i) gives
\[
\boxed{
(L,h)\text{ optimal }(m+n,b+q)
\ \Longrightarrow\
\bigl(R^q\pi_*(K_{X/Y}\otimes L),H\bigr)
\text{ optimal }(m,b).
}
\]

Here “optimal” means the following: for every positive auxiliary line bundle \((A,h_A)\) on \(Y\) and every compactly supported, smooth, \(\bar\partial\)-closed form
\[
f\in A_c^{a,b}(Y,\mathcal F\otimes A),
\]

there exists \(u\in L^2_{a,b-1}(Y,\mathcal F\otimes A)\) such that
\[
\bar\partial u=f,\qquad
\int_Y |u|^2_{H\otimes h_A,\omega_Y}\,dV_Y
\le
\int_Y
\left\langle B_Y^{-1}f,f\right\rangle_{H\otimes h_A,\omega_Y}\,dV_Y,
\tag{1}
\]

where
\[
B_Y=[\,i\Theta_{A,h_A}\otimes\operatorname{Id}_{\mathcal F},
       \Lambda_{\omega_Y}\,].
\]

The stated degree ranges ensure that \(B_Y>0\).

1. **When \(b=m\) and \(q=n\), no additional variation assumption is needed:**

2. **In range (i), a sufficient condition is**

   \boxed{\mu(y)+e(y)\ge 2m^2\kappa(y).}

   \[
   e(y)=\min_{\substack{\alpha\in\mathcal H_y^{p,q}\\\|\alpha\|=1}}

   Curvature compression and the fiber Bochner identity give the lower bound \(\mu+e\); the Gauss correction has norm at most \(2m^2\kappa\). Consequently,
   \[
   [i\Theta_H,\Lambda_Y]_{a,b}\ge0,
   \]
   which yields the required constant-one estimate.
